source: Moore (1985) The relationship between the originality of essays and variables in the problem-discovery process (ERIC ED258186), a replication of the Getzels still-life design with writers
finding: Closest thing found to a direct replication of the Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi design. Eight high-creative and eight low-creative middle school students arranged any of 15 objects on a table, then wrote an essay. Students judged creative handled and chose more, and rarer, objects. Their essays were rated more original.
numbers: N=16 (8 matched pairs). Problem-formulation total score: creative group mean 16.3 vs non-creative 3.0 (significant). Number of objects touched was significant. Two judge groups: originality and aesthetic value higher for the creative group in both; craftsmanship higher only for the second group. Judge-group agreement r=.92 originality, .82 craftsmanship, .75 aesthetic value (df=14). Grand process total vs originality r=.58. Originality-craftsmanship r=.66; originality-aesthetic r=.77.
limits: Group comparison on a pre-selected creative vs non-creative split, not a continuous sample. N=16. Originality, craftsmanship and aesthetic value correlate .66 to .82, so the product ratings may not be independent. Not peer reviewed (ERIC report).
agent_relevance: Gives full-text numbers for a replication in a different medium (writing) and age (about 12 to 14). Supports the idea that behaviour before committing (handling and trying many options) tracks later originality. Small human result; does not show an agent benefits.

source: Moore (1985) quoting Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976) The Creative Vision: scoring recipe and coefficients
finding: Moore reports how the 1976 study scored problem finding. Formulation score came from objects handled, uniqueness of objects chosen, and selection and arrangement of objects. Solution-stage scores came from photos every six minutes (openness of problem structure), discovery behaviour while drawing (switching media, pauses, substituting objects) and changes in problem structure. A 1 to 5 interview rating gave concern for discovery.
numbers: Grand total of process variables vs judged originality: r=.65 (N=31) per Moore. Unusualness score vs originality of the finished drawing: Pearson r=.42. Moore's own comparable r=.58.
limits: Second-hand: Moore cites the 1976 book, and in one place dates the original study 1964. Other secondary sources give other values (see d03). The book was not opened by this searcher.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 is half closed: a documented scoring recipe and two coefficients, but only through a replicator. For the agent, the scored behaviours (number of options handled, rarity of options, mid-task changes of framing) can be logged as process features of an open-mode phase.

source: Abdulla (2016, UGA dissertation) ch.3 reporting Csikszentmihalyi and Getzels (1971) J Pers Soc Psychol 19:47-52
finding: The dissertation describes the 1971 paper: five well-known artists and art critics rated each drawing for craftsmanship, originality and overall aesthetic value. Discovery-oriented behaviour at the formulation stage correlated with originality.
numbers: r=.54, p<.01 between concern for discovery at problem formulation and originality, as stated by Abdulla (2016). Moore gives .65 for a process total and .42 for unusualness (d02). A search snippet of the 1971 abstract page was cut off at a coefficient of 0.2 for overall aesthetic value (not verified).
limits: Three secondary sources give three different coefficients for related but not identical variable pairs. Which pair each belongs to cannot be settled without the primary text. Publisher full text is closed access; a full copy of the collected works on an unofficial host was deliberately not used.
agent_relevance: Do not quote a single 'Getzels r' in the schema notes. Safe wording: positive moderate correlations (about .4 to .65) in one sample of 31 art students, with craftsmanship not predicted.

source: Abdulla (2016) ch.3 moderator tables: age, domain, DT index, measure (meta-analysis, k=40 studies, 196 effects)
finding: Re-read the moderator tables for the age puzzle. Effects per age group: children (grades 1-6) 47, adolescents (grades 7-12) 26, adults 123. Adolescents are the weakest and also the smallest cell. Age is tangled with domain: age plus domain explain variance together and their interaction is not significant. Writing is the strongest domain.
numbers: Age Q(2)=6.60, p<.03: children r=.297 (CI .226-.365, 47 effects), adolescents r=.113 (CI .039-.185, 26 effects), adults r=.207 (CI .059-.345, 123 effects). DT index Q(3)=10.95 p<.01. Domain Q(4)=18.44 p<.001: writing .360 (14 effects, CI .243-.466), art .199 (33), science/math .162 (26), social/humanities .091 (49, CI -.213 to .379), other .282 (74). Gender Q(2)=1.69 p=.47, measure Q(3)=0.65 p=.88. Meta-regression age+domain QModel(2)=6.65 p<.05, interaction not significant. Female .305 vs male .183.
limits: Effects are nested inside 40 studies and treated as separate rows; independent studies per age cell are not given in the text read. The stated heterogeneity (I2 98.7%) and the very small residual Q in the regressions (QResidual(190)=188.53, p=.516) do not look consistent, so the regression tests deserve doubt. One dissertation, not the peer reviewed version.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. The adolescent dip is a thin, domain-confounded cell and no reason to design anything. Do not build an age-based rule.

source: Xie, Wang, Mallick, Sun, Noarov, Yu, Mallick, Dobriban (2026) Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models, arXiv 2602.13935 v3
finding: Closest test of gap 10. A reasoning model is stopped mid-trace when uncertainty keywords (such as 'missing', 'cannot determine') arrive too often, with the false-stop rate on well-posed questions calibrated on well-posed traces. Tested on 12 reasoning models. Two rules (Renewal, Maxwise) stop many ill-posed queries early and save 38 to 70 percent of tokens. The rule only halts; it does not turn the halt into a clarifying question.
numbers: Nominal false-positive target 5%. Last two table rows (Renewal / Maxwise): GSM-MC FPR 3.75% / 5.42%, power 69.75% / 70.92%; UMWP FPR 2.92% / 5.52%, power 46.78% / 48.65%; MiP FPR 1.12% / 3.21%, power 71.15% / 73.40%; MMLU FPR 0.75% / 2.63%, power 66.42% / 75.31%. Tokens saved on ill-posed queries, Renewal / Maxwise: GSM-MC 60.69 / 63.30%, UMWP 38.29 / 41.10%, MiP 62.78 / 68.15%, MMLU 58.80 / 69.83%. A length-only rule had power under one third. Prompt baselines (confidence dampening, critical reasoning) abstained on MiP items only 0.48 to 1.12% of the time.
limits: Uses keyword counts on open reasoning traces, so needs trace access. Needs a calibration set of well-posed traces. Short traces (UMWP) end before the first 250-token check. Table layout was garbled in extraction; row-to-method assignment was inferred from the paper text (Renewal lower FPR, Maxwise higher power). No clarifying question is generated and no end-task quality after asking is measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 is half closed. An early-exit rule on suspicion works and saves roughly 40 to 70 percent of tokens on ill-posed items with false stops of about 1 to 6 percent. The missing piece is the next step: route the stop to a question and check final answer quality. Lets S1 use a cheap trace monitor instead of a separate detector call.

source: Wang, McInerney, Wang, Kallus (2026) EAT: Entropy After </Think> for reasoning model early exiting, arXiv 2509.26522 v3
finding: General early-exit signal for reasoning models: append a stop-thinking token and watch the entropy of the next token; stop when its smoothed variance is low. Not about missing premises.
numbers: Token use down 12 to 22 percent on MATH-500 and AIME-2025 with no accuracy loss. Pass@1 often saturates within the first 10 to 20 percent of the token budget.
limits: Math only, well-posed questions. Nothing on ill-posed input or clarification. Needs logits or a proxy model.
agent_relevance: Sets the scale for generic early exit (12 to 22%), lower than the 38 to 70% that suspicion-based stopping saves on ill-posed items (d05). Different goal; do not mix the numbers.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2502.04485
finding: Direct test for gap 9. Instead of enumerating all hypotheses, the agent samples a few of its own candidate solutions, writes M=5 candidate questions, and picks the question whose answers split the sampled solutions most evenly (estimated information gain). Works in a game with no fixed answer list and on code tasks. The benefit shrinks for stronger models.
numbers: 20-questions style game: 15 target animals, 10 rounds, 5 seeds, guesses free over all animals (partition quality checked on a 500-animal list). EIG-uniform beat implicit and implicit-ToT question selection by a clear margin; EIG from log-probabilities was clearly worse than uniform weighting of samples. Code: 48 non-trivial HumanEval and APPS tasks, 4 elicited requirements, 3 seeds; EIG selection gave higher accuracy than zero-shot questions for Llama3-8B, GPT-3.5, Llama3-70B and GPT-4o-mini, with smaller gaps for stronger models. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini accuracy: 35% APPS vs 70% HumanEval. A diversity instruction raised sample diversity.
limits: Exact bar heights live in figures, not text. The user is simulated by an LLM or an executed program, so answers are noiseless. Costs more LLM calls than the baseline (appendix F); the authors argue the cost is small against the value of the answer. Tasks (animals, short functions) still have crisp answers.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap S1 or O8 step for open problems: sample 4 to 5 interpretations, write 5 questions, ask the one that best splits the interpretations. Needs a matched-token test against just asking the best single question, since the gain faded for stronger models.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: asking questions in Battleship with language-informed program sampling, arXiv 2402.19471
finding: Opened this time (earlier line c22 was snippet only). An LLM proposes questions, a program translates them, and expected information gain is computed exactly by running each question over every possible board. A few sampled questions reach human level. LLM-only baselines do not ground questions in the board.
numbers: Human questions: mean EIG 1.27 bits, best 3.61, 97% informative (EIG>0), 18 boards, 26 to 39 questions per board. Single LLM proposals (k=1): CodeLlama and GPT-4 mean EIG 0.65 to 0.66. At k=5 samples all models are roughly calibrated to the human average but fall short of the top 10 to 20 percent of human questions. The 0.99 seen earlier is a worked example in Figure 1, not a headline result.
limits: The hypothesis space is a finite board set that can be enumerated, so exact EIG is possible. That is exactly what open problems lack. The k comparison is in a figure; the text gives percentiles only roughly.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 answer in two parts: exact scoring works in closed worlds, and only sampled scoring is possible in open worlds (d07). Plan the agent's question scorer as sample-then-split, never as exact EIG.

source: Matsnev (2026) Uncertainty decomposition for clarification seeking in LLM agents, arXiv 2606.19559
finding: Prompt-only agents get a separate score for how underspecified the request is, apart from action confidence. On WebShop and ALFWorld variants where 50% of goals are underspecified, this raises clarification F1. But the extra check lowers average task success, and the author blames the shared reasoning budget (capability dilution).
numbers: Five backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B). Clarification F1 higher by about 0.28 absolute over ReAct+UE and 0.21 over UAM on average; ALFWorld-Clarification F1 +73% relative over ReAct+UE and +36% over UAM. Task success across all five benchmarks and backbones: 28.6% (ReAct+UE), 27.8% (UAM), 27.0% (proposed). REAL 32.1% to 19.2%; WebShop 31.9% to 26.1%; ALFWorld 57.5% to 58.9% (unchanged).
limits: Averages mix the standard (well specified) benchmarks with the clarification ones, so the success drop mostly measures the cost of carrying the check on well-specified tasks. Preprint, single author. The cause (budget split) is the author's reading; no ablation with extra tokens.
agent_relevance: Best available evidence on the false-alarm side of gap 3: an S1 check costs 0.8 to 1.6 points of success on average and 6 to 13 points on hard agent tasks when it shares the same pass. Argues for running the missing-info check as a separate cheap call, or only when a trigger fires, not inside the main reasoning pass.

source: Luo, Huang, Li, Meng, Liu, Hu, Feng, Liu (2025) ClarifyMT-Bench: benchmarking and improving multi-turn clarification, arXiv 2512.21120
finding: Non-code test of the ask-or-answer decision: 6,120 multi-turn dialogues with five kinds of ambiguity and six simulated user types. Ten LLMs lean toward answering too early, and accuracy falls with each turn. A four-module agent (perceive, forecast, track slots, plan) beat prompt baselines at the same number of passes.
numbers: Most models above 70% overall decision accuracy, with a steep drop by turn 2 and 3. Table 5 (accuracy by user type; P = precise user who has supplied the missing detail, so the right move is to stop asking). Llama-3.1-8B: base 48.3 on P, 71.2 average; majority vote 72.4 average; CoT 12.7 on P, 64.7 average; ClarifyAgent 58.0 on P, 88.4 average (15.4 above the best baseline at 73.0). Qwen-2.5-7B: base 96.6 on P, 57.9 average; CoT 66.4 average; ClarifyAgent 85.3 on P, 88.0 average. ClarifyAgent uses 5 forward passes, the same as majority voting with 5 samples. Large reasoning models did not beat instruction-tuned ones.
limits: Table text was garbled; row labels were inferred from the row count and from the paper's own 15.4-point statement. Simulated users. Over-clarification is measured after the user already supplied the detail, not on a fully specified first turn. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A non-code check that structure beats a bare prompt at equal passes (Qwen 88.0 vs 57.9 average) and a visible false-alarm cost for the decomposition on the stop-asking case (Qwen P 96.6 to 85.3). Gap 3 non-code replication of Edwards: partial yes, with a cost.

source: Fang, Jin, Dong, Li, Zhang, Jin, Li (2026) ClarifyCodeBench, arXiv 2607.00711
finding: Interactive code benchmark where each task hides part of the requirement. Models must decide whether the requirement is ambiguous, ask, then code. Questions are poor and late, and final code is worse than with the full requirement.
numbers: Best model (DeepSeek-V3.2): key-question rate (TKQR) 0.30 and optimal-round adherence (ORA) 0.50; most others under 0.30 TKQR and under 0.35 ORA. pass@1 with ambiguity is lower than with the full requirement by 7.8 to 19.8 points for every model.
limits: Code only. The metrics reward matching annotated key questions, which penalises valid alternative questions.
agent_relevance: A second code-side confirmation: missing information costs 8 to 20 points, so a detector has room to pay off on code. Does not answer the false-alarm part.

source: Nguyen, Tschiatschek, Singla (2026) Enhancing diversity of LLM-generated educational tasks (CreativeDC), arXiv 2512.23601 v2
finding: The only LLM test found of a diverge-then-converge prompt with blind experts. Stage 1: brainstorm unusual elements of the theme without the task constraints. Stage 2: pick one idea and build a valid task. Compared with a plain prompt and with think-step-by-step. About 1.6 times as many distinct high-utility tasks.
numbers: Qwen3-235B, temperature 1.0. At K=50 tasks: about 12 distinct high-utility tasks (Vendi, automated) vs about 8 for both baselines (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon). Expert clustering: about 16 vs 9 clusters. Three expert raters, one concept (Variables), 20 blind novelty pairs: CreativeDC won 96.67% (SE 2.32), interestingness 0.81 vs 0.50, task validity 1.00 vs 0.78. Utility judged by Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite.
limits: Tokens not matched (the two-stage prompt writes a brainstorm first). One model, one domain (Python practice tasks), three experts who each saw different themes, so no inter-rater agreement. Diversity of tasks is not problem finding.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly informed: a forced explore-first phase beat commit-first on diversity and blind novelty in one small human-rated test. Equal-token comparison and open-ended agent tasks remain untested.

source: Tutone, Franceschelli, Musolesi (2026) The limits of automatic evaluation of creativity in LLMs, arXiv 2608.23705
finding: Blind human ratings of 100 human and 100 AI short stories on 11 creativity dimensions, compared with automatic metrics and an LLM judge. Humans saw little difference between the two sets. The LLM judge scored AI stories higher on all dimensions and gave perfect 5.0 to many. Automatic metrics had near-zero alignment with humans.
numbers: Judge: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct; stories from GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, Mistral Large 3, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro. Human creativity means 3.16 (human texts) vs 3.27 (AI), p=.569. Judge vs human on human-written stories, Kendall tau: Elaboration .31 (p<.001), Creativity .23, Novelty .17 (p=.042), Surprise -.01 (p=.867), Effectiveness .13 and Usefulness .08 (not significant). Perplexity vs Effectiveness rho=-.23; best metric correlation .29 (POS variance vs Elaboration).
limits: Short stories, one open-weight judge, human rater count not read. Not a test of reframing.
agent_relevance: Supports not using an LLM judge as the only scorer of reframe quality (gap 4). Even an unrelated-family judge gave tau of about 0 to 0.3 with humans. Use judge scores only as a screen, with human or downstream checks.

source: Shypula, Li, Zhang, Padmakumar, Yin, Bastani (2025) Evaluating the diversity and quality of LLM generated content (effective semantic diversity), COLM 2025, arXiv 2504.12522
finding: Proposes counting only distinct outputs that pass a quality bar. On tasks with an executable check, preference-tuned models give more effective diversity than SFT or base models even though raw diversity is lower. A cheap proxy that needs no human and no judge.
numbers: Metric: number of semantically distinct generations among those meeting a quality threshold, with quality from execution tests on code and verified answers. Per the abstract, larger models give higher effective diversity, while smaller models are more parameter-efficient.
limits: Quality gate needs a verifiable task, which most reframing tasks lack. No validation against human ratings of reframes. Only the abstract, introduction and metric definition were read.
agent_relevance: Candidate answer to gap 4: score a reframe by how many distinct, downstream-solvable solution paths it opens, with a dedupe count and a pass/fail gate. Needs a test against human ranks on reframing tasks before use.

source: Bisconti et al. (2025/2026) Adversarial poetry as a universal single-turn jailbreak mechanism in LLMs, arXiv 2511.15304 v3
finding: Closest measured case of reframing changing harm rate: keeping the same harmful intent but rewriting the request as verse raised attack success. Style and frame shifts alone move safety behaviour.
numbers: 25 frontier models. 20 hand-written poems: average attack success 62%. 1,200 MLCommons prompts converted to verse by a meta-prompt: ASR 8.08% (prose) to 43.07% (verse), up to 18 times higher on single models. Judges: ensemble of three open-weight LLMs (majority vote), validated with 2,100 human labels over 600 outputs.
limits: An attack that reframes the user request, not an agent reframing its own task. Does not measure constraint violations in benign tasks. Judge-based labels.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open but with a warning: an O8 reframe that changes style or abstraction might lower safeguards. Needs a direct harm and constraint-violation count with and without O8 on benign tasks.

source: Tool-framing bypasses LLM safety: procedural abstraction reduces refusal rates by up to 40 points (ICML 2026 listing, abstract only)
finding: Seen only as a conference abstract in a search result. Recasting harmful requests as sequences of tool calls lowers refusal in agent setups.
numbers: 1,040 matched prompt pairs, 13 harm categories, 3 models. Refusal drops 10.9 to 40.2 points. GPT-OSS-20b 85.2% to 45.0%; DeepSeek-Chat 76.9% to 46.3%; Claude Sonnet 4.5 80.7% to 69.9%. McNemar p<0.001 each.
limits: Abstract only, not opened. Adversarial framing, not benign reframing.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as d15 for agent form: a change of frame or form can lower refusal. A lead, not evidence of an O8 harm rate.

source: Williamson, Ji, Dwyer (2025) Syntactic blind spots: how misalignment leads to LLMs' mathematical errors, arXiv 2510.01831
finding: Rewording an already-failed math question into the structure of correctly answered questions often fixes the answer. Gains are larger on narrative or varied phrasing (GSM8K, SVAMP) and smaller on uniform sets (MultiArith, ASDiv). A boundary: reformulation helps when surface form is the obstacle.
numbers: Five open-source LLMs, four math datasets. Recovered answers from 2 (Qwen on MultiArith) to 210 (Gemma on ASDiv); accuracy gain up to 15.5% (Granite on MultiArith). Weaker models (Gemma, Granite) gained most.
limits: Only questions the model first got wrong were rephrased, so regression to the mean inflates the recovery (some would flip on a plain resample); no resample control seen in the parts read. Math word problems, not open problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 boundary: a surface restate can help, not through insight but because the model's habits suit one form. Predicts gains for weak models on varied phrasing and little for strong models on well-formed tasks, in line with step-back and Shin.

source: CRTBench logical reformulation consistency (search-result summary of arXiv 2607.14528, Controlled Reformulation Testing)
finding: Seen only in a search summary. Logically equivalent rewrites split into surface rewrites (models robust) and logically nontrivial ones such as contrapositive and double negation (models fail more).
numbers: As summarised: GPT-5.4-mini 98.9% base accuracy but 60.3% family-level consistency; contrapositive 72.4%, double negation 84.6%; surface rewrites 94 to 100%; more reasoning effort lifted consistency to 85.4%.
limits: Not opened; numbers come from a search summary. Tests consistency under equivalent rewrites, not reframing for creativity.
agent_relevance: If true, an O8 reframe that changes logical form risks changing the answer; keep a check that the reframed problem keeps the original stated constraints.

source: Search record for gaps 1, 6 and 8 (this session): no paired test found
finding: Searches for an equal-token test of an explicit open-mode phase against commit-first with blind human raters, for a measured harm or constraint-violation rate with and without a reframe step, and for a structured frame template vs a plain restate at equal tokens found nothing beyond sources already in the file (b14, b16) plus CreativeDC (d12).
numbers: 0 new direct tests for the three comparisons. Related but not matching: CreativeDC (diversity), adversarial reframing studies (d15, d16).
limits: A negative search result with limited tools (arXiv keyword API returned little; OpenAlex refused anonymous access). Absence from search is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: These three experiments must be built by us if we want answers; nothing in the literature can be borrowed.
